content.title: About
content.content: Lebkuchen is a traditional German cookie made with honey, spices, nuts, and dried fruit. The dough is soft and aromatic, while the finished treat has a crisp edge and a gently spiced flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lebkuchen originated in medieval monasteries as an energy snack for fasting monks.
Typical ingredients include almonds, hazelnuts, raisins, and orange zest.
Regional variations exist: Bavarian recipes add ginger, Thuringian versions use cardamom.
The cookies are often glazed with powdered sugar to resemble snow.
Around Christmas, lebkuchen is considered a symbol of warmth and coziness.

items.title: Rich in nuts and dried fruit
items.content: Nuts and dried fruit provide healthy fats, vitamins, and minerals.

items.title: Contains honey
items.content: Honey offers antioxidant properties and may support immune function.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Spice content
items.content: Ginger, cinnamon, and clove have anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of carbs and fats makes lebkuchen a quick source of energy.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Lebkuchen contains almonds and hazelnuts, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Honey and added sugar make the cookie calorie‑dense; moderation is advised.

items.title: Gluten presence
items.content: The dough is usually wheat‑based, unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Some recipes use lemon juice; individuals with acid reflux should be cautious.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lebkuchen can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, served with tea or coffee, used in dessert platters, or crumbled over yogurt or ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store lebkuchen in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent moisture‑related spoilage.
